summary: In Greek mythology, Agapenor was the leader of the Arcadians in the Trojan War. A son of Ancaeus and grandson of Lycurgus, he reigned as king of Arcadia and was numbered among the suitors of Helen. He received sixty ships from Agamemnon to carry his landlocked Arcadians to Troy, and was among the warriors hidden inside the Trojan Horse. On the voyage home a storm drove him to Cyprus, where he founded the city of Paphos and built its famous temple of Aphrodite.

sections.heading: Family
paragraphs: Agapenor was a son of Ancaeus and a grandson of Lycurgus of Arcadia. Through this line he belonged to the royal house of Arcadia and ruled as its king.
He had a descendant named Laodice, who was remembered for sending a robe (peplos) as a gift to Athena Alea at Tegea, and for building a temple of Aphrodite Paphia there.

sections.heading: Trojan War
paragraphs: Agapenor appeared among the suitors of Helen, the gathering of Greek princes who sought her hand and were afterward bound to support her chosen husband.
As king of the Arcadians, Agapenor received sixty ships from Agamemnon, in which he led his Arcadians to Troy. He was also counted among the warriors who hid inside the Trojan Horse.

sections.heading: Cyprus and Paphos
paragraphs: On Agapenor's return from Troy he was cast by a storm onto the coast of Cyprus. There he founded the town of Paphos, and in it the famous temple of Aphrodite.

sections.heading: Other traditions
paragraphs: Agapenor also figures in the story of Alcmaeon: it was to him that Arsinoe (also called Alphesiboea), Alcmaeon's wife, was sold away by her own brothers.
